data.title: Netflix Stock Is Down 40%. Can Q3 Earnings Spark a Comeback?
data.description:
A little over a year ago, Netflix (NFLX) stock was still riding high, trading just off record highs and lording over all other competitors in the streaming-video space it still dominates. Then came a big third-quarter earnings miss. Then a failed bid to buy Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD). Then another earnings miss this spring. Add it all up, and NFLX shares have fallen 40% in the last 12 months.

Is a turnaround imminent? That likely depends on next Tuesday’s (October 20) third-quarter earnings results – at least in the short term.

Another miss or microscopic bottom-line beat – the only two scenarios the company has mustered in each of the last four quarters – could send shares tumbling right back to their lows around 67 (they currently trade in the 72 range), or possibly lower. Another narrow beat, like it produced in the second quarter and in the fourth quarter of 2025, and the stock may continue to stagnate.

But a convincing beat? That could be a game changer.

NFLX Now a Value Stock

After all, despite the series of underwhelming earnings reports and the humiliation of having its apparent winning Warner Bros. bid snatched away by a higher hostile takeover bid from Paramount Skydance, Netflix is doing just fine. The streamer is tracking toward 13.4% revenue growth and 41.5% earnings growth this year. Those compare favorably to 16.5% sales growth and 27.5% EPS growth in 2025. The business isn’t really slowing. And yet, one of the market’s great growth stocks over the last decade-plus is being treated like it has leprosy.

[text_ad]

That makes it a value play. But it also is in desperate need of a catalyst.

Part of the disappointment surrounding the company’s last two earnings reports is not what Netflix said, but what it didn’t say. Namely – how it plans to spend the $83 billion earmarked for the Warner Bros. deal that it ended up having to pocket. Sure, there have been some half-measures – it forked over $200 million to buy the rights to next summer’s Women’s Soccer World Cup and paid an undisclosed amount to air some matches at the Men’s World Cup in 2030 in Spain and Andorra. But the streamer hasn’t made a big, Warner Bros.-like splash. If anything, it’s continuing to save, cutting roughly 1,000 jobs – or 6% of its workforce – this week in its biggest staff reduction since 2022. Wall Street seemed to like the move – NFLX shares were up nearly 3% on Thursday as of this writing. But it’s the latest and most egregious example of the streamer’s sudden austerity and purse-tightening, at a time when many investors have been expecting them to splurge.

Perhaps Netflix is saving for the next big fish. My guess is it will be a major sports property of some kind. As the two new World Cup deals and this summer’s airing of Major League Baseball’s Home Run Derby reveal, Netflix clearly sees live sports as an increasingly vital revenue stream that it has rarely tapped into until recently. For the past two Christmases, it has aired two NFL games, and last month it aired an opening-week NFL game for the first time. I think there’s a lot more coming, maybe something along the lines of Amazon Prime Video’s Thursday Night Football deal or Apple TV’s Friday Night Baseball package.

Netflix Earnings: What to Expect

Nothing seems imminent, though, and I doubt a “big” announcement will be part of next week’s earnings call. Instead, the results may have to speak for themselves. The bar is set fairly high: EPS estimates of 82 cents would mark a 39% improvement over the 59 cents the streamer earned in the third quarter a year ago. To get investors back on board in droves, Netflix will likely need to top that 82-cent estimate by more than a penny or two.

Even absent the first definitive earnings beat in more than a year, I love the stock’s upside from here. It currently trades at a mere 18.7x forward earnings estimates, barely more than half its five-year average valuation and a fraction of the 52x forward P/E it was going for in summer 2025. NFLX has rarely been cheaper. And yet, the company is on track for record sales and earnings this year, with EPS potentially being double what it was in 2024.

That’s a recipe for a monster bounce-back. Now the stock just needs a spark. Perhaps next week’s earnings can provide it.

[author_ad]

data.title: How to Handle the Hidden Bear Market
data.description:
The stock market and the economy now face significant challenges. So, it is no surprise that the majority of stocks are in a bear market, or at least a correction. When the market is in a steep sell-off like this, it is tough to know when it will bottom.

I know what you are thinking: “What bear market? The S&P 500 keeps hitting new highs.”

This is true. But it is only part of the story.

Under the hood, more than 70% of S&P 500 stocks were recently at least 10% below their recent highs, notes technical analyst Jason Goepfert, who founded SentimenTrader. Close to 60% of S&P 500 components were recently in a bear market, meaning a 20% or more drawdown, notes Lawrence McDonald of The Bear Traps Report.

In short, there is a stealth, internal correction. The S&P 500 is being propped up by a few strong names in AI.

[text_ad]

Looked at it a different way, the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (RSP) was recently 6.6% off its high, while the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) continues to hit new highs. Yes, a 6.6% decline is not a 10% correction. But keep in mind, the equal-weight ETF is being propped up by a handful of AI names, as well.

What’s going on?

It is possible that the internal correction is the market already pricing in at least some of the upcoming economic weakness that Jim Paulsen of Paulsen Perspectives on Substack has been predicting. While the economy continues to produce OK growth, he posits that high oil prices, high yields and the strong dollar, among other factors, are all putting downward pressure on growth.

Another problem for stocks is that earnings estimate revision momentum is slowing, notes Nick Raich at The Earnings Scout. The momentum slowed in the second quarter. It is slowing even more among the early Q3 reporters. When this momentum slows for two quarters in a row while the S&P 500 continues higher, it normally does not end well, says Raich. Typically, a correction or worse follows.

The tricky part now is that much of the market already has corrected, suggesting that at least part of the estimate revisions momentum slowdown and the potential economic slowdown is already getting priced in.

On the other hand, investors are complacent. Complacent investors are vulnerable to “surprise” in response to any stock weakness among the tech leaders. Selling can compound selling when investors are complacent. The Investors Intelligence Bull/Bear ratio recently came in at 3.62. This signals complacency, which makes the market vulnerable to selling. Investors are complacent because they are paying more attention to the S&P 500 hitting new highs, rather than the internal correction that is playing out.

Here’s the bottom line for me. Despite these risks (potential economic slowdown per Paulsen, revisions momentum slowdown a la Raich, investor complacency), starting to average down in a 10%-20% decline has been a successful tactic in the past, even if it inevitably means being early. Just plan purchases in several phases. Also note that October 12 on average tends to be the low for the year, and it typically marks the end of the traditional September-October market weakness phase.

Insiders are generally now under broad trading lockdowns ahead of earnings season. But executives and directors at several companies have recently made bullish purchases nevertheless. For detailed analysis of their companies and the catalysts that might make their stocks go up, consider subscribing to Cabot Insider Edge.

data.title: Are Fears Over High Bond Yields Overblown?
data.description:
Bonds have a reputation for being stodgy and boring; as such, they’re not normally on the tips of investors’ tongues when talking about markets. But when bonds are suddenly the talk of the town, it’s not usually a good sign for stocks.

It happens that now is one of those rare times when bonds are getting lots of attention, and not because bond prices are levitating. Instead, rising bond yields are the focus, with the benchmark 10-year Treasury Yield Index (TNX) recently hitting its highest level since April 2002, at just over 5.3%.

This level carries a deep psychological significance for investors since TNX experienced a sustained rise above that level that accompanied the dot-com bubble collapse and subsequent bear market. It’s a level that has served as a bearish catalyst—or at least a major headwind—for equities over much of the past quarter of a century.

What’s more, TNX briefly hitting 5.3% in mid-2007 arguably increased selling pressures and served as a catalyst, or at least an accelerant, for the credit crisis that followed. With this background in mind, it’s understandable that investors are concerned over the latest yield spike to the much-feared 5.3% level.

[text_ad]

As contrarians, however, this naturally begs the question: Are the fears over high bond yields overblown? After all, 10-year yields considerably above 5.3% commonly prevailed in decades prior to the 2000s—even as stock prices remained elevated. Therefore, a case could be made that investors’ fears over current bond yield levels are misplaced and based more on the arguably abnormally low bond yields of the last couple of decades, rather than on the historical norm.

The Contrarian Case That High Bond Yields Are Nothing to Fear

That’s precisely the argument that Wall Street economist Ed Yardeni has made in stating his case that current bond market worries are exaggerated, with bonds likely near a turning point. To underscore his case, he pointed out that this week’s edition of The Economist features the headline, “Will bonds blow up?” on the front cover. The so-called “front cover indicator” is well known to contrarian investors, who recognize that whenever an established market trend makes the cover of a mainstream magazine, it’s often a sign that the trend has reached its terminus.

Yardeni makes the case that this is likely true for the bond yield rally, with investors likely having “moved on,” in his words. He further writes: “We think the 10-year Treasury bond yield is back to normal this year, i.e., in the 4.00% to 5.00% range.”

He further argues that the popular “higher for longer” argument that interest rates are likely to remain elevated—which in turn suggests they’ll come back down—is erroneous. Instead, Yardeni maintains that “interest rates are likely to stay normal for longer.”

In other words, the exceptionally low interest rates that prevailed following the 2008 financial crisis and before the pandemic were the historical anomaly, in his view, and investors should therefore prepare for a sustained period of more historically normal yields. That means stronger demand for bonds at higher yields helping to keep the 10-year Treasury yield within his projected 4%–5% range.

My view largely aligns with Yardeni’s, though I see the potential for higher yields in the coming years as the secular inflation cycle continues to exert its influence. But from a near-term perspective, I think Yardeni is likely to be proven correct, with TNX pulling back from its multi-decade high over the next few months.

If that indeed proves to be the case, it should prove beneficial for equity prices. And I think that can be considered a contrarian signal for investors as we head further into the normally bullish Q4.

[author_ad]

data.title: What’s Behind the Drop in Fair Isaac (FICO)?
data.description:
Key Takeaways

  • FICO’s monopoly is under threat. New federal rules are opening the mortgage credit-scoring market to competition.
  • FICO could lose its pricing power. Competitors are offering cheaper alternatives, threatening the company’s high profit margins.
  • The stock’s future is uncertain. FICO remains highly profitable, but investors are questioning whether its incredible growth can continue.

At the time of writing, shares of Fair Isaac Corp. (FICO) are down 57.3% in 2026, including multiple one-day double-digit declines in the last three months and a massive 26.5% drop on September 29 alone.

What’s notable about it isn’t necessarily the scale of the decline (there are actually 10 large-cap stocks that have lost more than 50% year to date) but the reason behind it: We’re seeing in real time what happens when a company’s moat dries up.

[text_ad]

FICO’s Incredible Business Model

Odds are good that you’re intimately familiar with the company’s product (and its ticker symbol), even if you’ve never heard the name “Fair Isaac.” It’s the company behind the FICO credit score, the three-digit number lenders use to judge a borrower’s creditworthiness.

For decades, FICO has dominated the credit-scoring business. And its greatest advantage has been in the mortgage market.
Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the government-backed companies that buy and guarantee a huge share of U.S. mortgages, have long required lenders to use FICO scores.

That essentially gave Fair Isaac a government-supported monopoly – or, in more charitable terms, an insurmountable moat.

Mortgage lenders couldn’t simply switch to a cheaper competitor. They had to use FICO if they wanted to sell their loans to Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac.

That gave FICO tremendous pricing power. It could steadily raise prices without worrying about losing customers.

And because producing an additional credit score costs very little, those price increases translated into huge profits.

Investors loved the business. Even factoring in the latest decline, shares are up 484% in the last decade. But new rule changes are forcing a re-rate of the stock.

The Government Opens the Door to Competition

The biggest threat comes from VantageScore, a competing credit-scoring system created by Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.

VantageScore has been around for years. But until recently, it couldn’t compete effectively in the mortgage market because federal rules favored FICO.

That started to change in 2022, when the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) approved newer scoring models from both companies.

Then, in July 2025, regulators announced that mortgage lenders could use VantageScore 4.0 instead of traditional FICO scores for eligible loans sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac (about 70% of mortgages).

The changes accelerated in 2026.

In April, federal housing officials moved forward with VantageScore’s adoption. And on September 9, the FHFA opened VantageScore to all approved Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac lenders.

Then came another major blow.

On September 30, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac announced changes that would put FICO and VantageScore on equal footing, removing a scoring “edge” that had previously favored FICO scores over VantageScore.

Why These Changes Are Such a Big Deal

It’s not often that investors see the impact of a government-mandated monopoly being opened to the free market.

Now that Fair Isaac is facing actual competition, it’ll be forced to compete on a slew of fronts, most importantly, cost – which is where the competition is focusing its efforts.

TransUnion recently announced that it would extend its $0.99 VantageScore pricing through December 2028, a fraction of the price of Fair Isaac’s scoring.

Meanwhile, FICO has historically used regular price increases to drive much of its growth.

In its fiscal third quarter, FICO’s business-to-business scoring revenue jumped 49% from a year earlier, largely because of higher mortgage-score prices.

But now that the company faces the prospect of competing on prices, the stock is in uncharted waters, and there are threats to the underlying business model.

Rocket Mortgage, one of the country’s largest mortgage lenders, has already announced plans to make VantageScore its preferred scoring model for eligible loans.

And from the end of May through the end of August, 9% of the mortgages originated used VantageScore.

Beyond the immediate threat, there is also a possibility that Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae could throw their own hats (Freddie Score and Fannie Score) into the ring as competitors in the marketplace.

Fair Isaac, as one might expect, isn’t taking the news lying down. Last year, the company introduced a new licensing program designed to lower costs, and it is presumably looking for longer-term fixes to make its offerings more competitive.

And the reality is that the company still has major advantages. Its credit scores are widely trusted, lenders have used them for decades, and its software business provides another source of revenue.

It’s also far too early to know how much market share VantageScore will capture. Nine percent penetration is notable, and it reflects impressive growth, but it’s still just a fraction of the total market.

But even if FICO keeps most of its customers, losing the ability to raise prices aggressively could significantly slow earnings growth.

Given the volatility in the stock (down more than 70% from its all-time highs in 2024) and the major disruption it faces, investors should approach the stock with caution and look for evidence that VantageScore’s penetration is plateauing, while also keeping in mind that Fannie and Freddie may be waiting in the wings to further pressure the company.

[author_ad]

data.title: How We Rode STMicroelectronics (STM) to a Double in 2 Months
data.description:
The basic premise of trading momentum stocks is that strength begets strength. A stock that is performing well and showing signs of accumulation is likely to outperform other stocks that are not.

Outperformance in bull markets leads to outsized gains, while outperformance in weak markets can be a sign that investors are using the shakier backdrop to buy shares at a discount (that’s the short version of why we include relative performance in our technical criteria).

Identifying those kinds of stocks is the bread and butter of our Cabot Momentum Trader advisory, so I wanted to walk through a recent winning trade in STMicroelectronics (STM) from earlier this year to show exactly how it’s done.

Of course, not every stock that shows promise will go on to double in two months, but in a market that’s sharply divided between winners and losers, it’s important to identify the stocks with that kind of potential.

[text_ad]

Chief Analyst Mike Cintolo notifies Cabot Momentum Trader subscribers of the 10 best-looking stocks on Monday of every week. Of those 10 picks, he also highlights a “Top Pick,” which is the most promising of the group.

Mike prioritizes stocks with compelling stories that the market has latched onto, solid fundamentals, and impressive technical strength.

The Monday issues also include a full list of every stock that’s currently being covered, as well as stocks that are being dropped from coverage because they either failed to break out or no longer meet Mike’s criteria.

Here’s how he described STMicroelectronics on April 6, 2026.

… for our Top Pick, we’re going with growth—STMicroelectronics (STM) is a chipmaker with its hands in many cookie jars, but it looks like it’s finally catching a hold of the AI bandwagon, which should drive margins higher. Shares broke out today.

STMicroelectronics (STM) ★ Top Pick ★

Why the Strength

Dutch chipmaker STMicroelectronics is primed to be a major beneficiary of the $700 billion capital expenditures AI hyperscalers have announced for 2026. STM’s products address many of the steps in running an AI data center such as converting power at the server and converting electronic signals to light for optical data transmission. Management believes it can sell $500 million of goods into AI data centers this year and more than $1 billion next, partially thanks to a recently announced multiyear deal with Amazon Web Services to develop advanced semiconductors in what STM says is a “multi-billion-dollar” commercial deal. The company is also developing high-efficiency chips on silicon alternatives including gallium nitride and silicon carbide that are better suited to handle the high heat generated by intense AI operations. STM is gearing up production of silicon photonics products to feed the AI market this year, opening a 300-millimeter wafer production plant in Crolles, France, part of $2 billion in spending it will do this year. Other partnerships should also lead to strong AI-focused products, including an agreement inked with Nvidia last year to develop a new 800-volt DC power architecture. While investors are focused on AI for growth, STMicro feeds a number of industries, with 84% of Q4 2025’s $3.3 billion sales coming in areas like automotive, personal electronics and industrial, which account for 38%, 26% and 20% of revenue, respectively. Those industries are mixed, with auto down 15% last year, personal electronics up 17% and industrial up 5%. But the enthusiasm for the stock is all about AI, which will be a growing piece of the pie from here. For Q1, ended March, STM probably will see revenue jump 20% to over $3 billion, generating earnings per share of $0.17. Full-year sales may be constrained by lack of capacity, with consensus expecting a 14% rise to $13.4 billion, though analysts see margins and earnings skyrocketing both this year and next.

Technical Analysis

STM was a big laggard over the past couple of years, with an ugly long-term decline into last April’s low, and even after an oversold recovery, shares didn’t make much progress for the next few months. But the action improved after the November low, with shares actually popping to marginal new highs in early February after its expanded deal with Amazon. And now, after hacking sideways for a few weeks, STM actually broke out today. Of course, breakouts often run into some wobbles in rough markets, but we’re OK with a small position here or (preferably) on dips.

data.title: Is the Stock Market Ready for a Big Breakout? AI Stocks Could Lead the Way
data.description:
It’s been a tricky environment for months, with an ever-larger number of crosscurrents popping up in the news (oil prices and interest rates versus accelerating AI investment) and the market itself (weak broad market, though big-cap indexes are actually kissing new high ground). Thus, we thought it’d be a good get Mike Cintolo, Cabot’s Chief Investment Strategist, on the horn and see what he’s making of all this mixed messaging.

[text_ad]

Brad: Mike–good to talk to you again. Let’s start with the overall picture and what your general view is of where we are and where you think things might be headed.

Mike: Frankly, it’s been as mixed a market as I can remember in my 27-plus years here, with the evidence pointing in all different directions. Recently, we saw our Cabot Tides, which measures the market’s intermediate-term trend, turn down, and just days later, our Aggression Index, which measures growth stocks vs. defensive stocks, turn bullish.

Even beyond the market action, many things that usually swim together aren’t doing so now. For instance, very few stocks have been hitting 52-week highs for weeks and weeks, which is an indirect sign of negative sentiment—but if you look at most sentiment measures, they’re not showing much panic, with a few even showing investor optimism.

All that said, I am encouraged overall because of the setup and the growth evidence—I still expect the next big move to be up, and that could be starting now, as we’ve seen the S&P and Nasdaq perk up. We did do some buying in Cabot Growth Investor’s Model Portfolio this week for the first time in many weeks, but we’re also still holding a good amount of cash, waiting for a broader, clearer liftoff.

Brad: Can you talk more about that last point, specifically the setup? What’s looking encouraging now versus, say, a few months ago?

Mike: It’s really the interplay of growth and risk-on names compared to stodgy areas of the market. A few months ago, the Nasdaq was fading after a huge April-May run, while the Dow Industrials were hitting new highs and the broad market was strong—a lot of market pundits said that action is good, that “rotation is the lifeblood of a bull market,” but in reality that setup rarely works. What was really happening was that big investors were selling leaders and buying laggards, and sure enough, those gains everyone was excited about in June and July evaporated in August and September.

Today, though, the situation is the opposite: The Nasdaq is the strongest major index, growth funds are outperforming the broad market and the Dow Industrials is relatively weak—all while there’s plenty of worrisome news. Don’t misunderstand me, I’m not rooting for a weak broad market, but this sort of setup usually leads to far better performance going ahead than the opposite.

Brad: I understand what you’re saying. But my bigger question is, given this setup, what action would have you turning fully bullish?

Mike: That’s easy—simply more strength in the market as a whole, as well as the stocks I own and am watching. I mentioned the small number of new highs earlier; on the S&P 500 and NYSE, the 50-day moving average is at 16-month lows. I’d like to see the general new high list pick up, led by growth stocks that have spent many months building fresh launching pads. I’ve seen a bit of that, but for every name or two that perks up, there are at least that many still seeing selling on strength.

Brad: Before we dive into stocks and sectors, I have to ask you about interest rates, which are obviously moving up and in the headlines most days. Any thoughts?

Mike: In terms of rates themselves, all I’ll really say is the trend is clearly up, though there’s so much attention being paid to rates that I do wonder if it’s time for a rest, at least for a few weeks. But other than that, I’m really focused more on the market itself.

Brad: OK, let’s get into the good stuff—where are you seeing opportunities these days, and what looks ready to lead if this market really gets going?

Mike: Well, AI has been the leader since 2023, and I don’t think that’s set to change—however, what does change is the names, as different subgroups have taken the baton. Right now, I’m increasingly excited about agentic AI, which has been gaining traction with businesses all year, but now, with Meta’s Muse [a personal AI agent launched in September that’s become the most downloaded app], seems to have hit the mainstream with consumers. That has big investors discounting the future where millions of these agents will be figuratively running around to research, notify and transact in the months ahead.

Brad: What stocks or sectors are in favor with agentic AI?

Mike: I just wrote about this last week in Cabot Growth Investor, so I don’t want to give away the store—but I’ll say that cybersecurity in general will be important to prevent agents from going where they’re not supposed to; web traffic should boom as agents constantly and automatically scour the web; and CPUs will be key on the infrastructure side. There are many names in each theme acting well, and that’s just for agentic AI, though I do think that is positioned to be the leading theme here if we get a bull run.

Brad: Fair enough, but can you at least throw a couple of names our way?

Mike: Well, Cloudflare (NET) is a name we’ve owned in the Model Portfolio for a while and continues to act well, and should play into both web traffic and security for agentic AI. Moreover, with all things chips still doing well, a name like Taiwan Semi (TSM) is doing well—actually moving to new highs last week ahead of most things.

Brad: Great, thanks. Any final words of wisdom before we finish up?

Mike: Only that I think we’re getting close to “decision time” for the market, simply because it’s spent most of the past year doing nothing—from last November through March, and then from June through today, the indexes have been net losers; the April-May boomlet had all the net gains and more. Thus, while I do think we could have another wobble or two, my guess is a big move is coming—and the odds favor it being up. So have your shopping list ready.

[author_ad]

data.title: Situational Awareness Adds Leverage the Right Way
data.description:
Just over two months ago, “whiz kid” Leopold Aschenbrenner’s hedge fund Situational Awareness “blew up” via a grossly over-leveraged portfolio of AI stocks. The fund had been borrowing heavily to size up its AI bets, and when the group cracked in July, margin calls forced it to sell the bulk of its stock portfolio to Citadel in a roughly $16 billion block. JPMorgan then cut off its lending relationship with the fund.

So, when CNBC’s David Faber reported in mid-September that Situational Awareness was adding bullish exposure again, but this time via the options market, it lined up with something I’d already been watching build in the options world.

Here is what I mean …

The Call Buying

Faber reported the fund had been adding bullish exposure to AMD, BE, CRWV, SKHY and SNDK. And not surprisingly, I’d seen call buying in nearly all of these names in the prior week, but until then I hadn’t been able to nail down who the buyer was.
Once the report hit, it became somewhat obvious, as you can see via these trades:

  • Buyer of 2,000 CoreWeave (CRWV) March 145 Calls for $8.40 – Stock at 89
  • Buyer of 1,700 Bloom Energy (BE) November 250 Calls for $25.10 – Stock at 217
  • Buyer of 2,000 SK Hynix (SKHY) December 240 Calls for $13.65 – Stock at 186
  • Buyer of 1,600 Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) February 650 Calls for $39.65 – Stock at 507

That’s roughly $15 million on these four trades alone … and the fund didn’t slow down.

A week later, traders flagged another roughly $96 million in short-dated SanDisk, Micron, Intel and Marvell calls, all expiring October 2, that many on the Street suspected came from the same desk.

[text_ad]

Leverage the Right Way … Sort Of

I’m encouraged that the fund swapped borrowed money for calls. With options, the most you can lose is the premium paid. No margin calls, and no forced fire sale to Citadel.

That being said, I don’t love how far out-of-the-money so many of these call buys were. Maybe I should let this rocket scientist know that the best way to get leverage to a stock is to buy IN-the-money calls, not OUT-of-the-money calls.

Here’s why. The CRWV March 145 calls need the stock to rally more than 70% just to break even. An in-the-money call, on the other hand, moves closer to dollar for dollar with the stock and doesn’t need a moonshot to pay off. You still get the leverage … without needing to be perfectly right on both direction and timing.

One Bet the Other Way

Finally, one stock we know Situational Awareness had been betting against is Adobe (ADBE), which is assumed to be a company/stock that could be at risk if the AI theme plays out. And right on cue, as the trader was buying pro-AI stocks, a trader stepped in with these puts looking for downside:

  • Buyer of 1,500 Adobe (ADBE) June 260 Puts for $39.50 – Stock at 251

Interestingly, this one IS in-the-money, as the 260 strike sits $9 above where the stock was trading. That’s roughly $5.9 million in premium, with a breakeven of 220.50, or about 12% below the stock price.

Lesson Learned

You don’t need a multi-billion-dollar fund to learn from this. Situational Awareness found out the hard way that margin can wipe you out in a matter of weeks. Calls and puts, on the other hand, give you leverage with a hard cap on what you can lose, which is exactly why they’re the foundation of everything we do at Cabot Options Trader.

data.title: Midterms & the Stock Market—What to Expect
data.description:
I love fall! But one thing I don’t look forward to is the midterm elections and the hateful ads that infiltrate the media during this time of year. But unless I want to run for office (which I do not!), the only thing I can do to initiate any governmental change is to VOTE, and I encourage you to do just that!

Another step you may want to take during this time is to look over your portfolio to see if you need to make any changes/additions/deletions to investments that may be affected by the outcome of the midterm elections.

[text_ad]

The good news, as you can see in the chart below, according to research by Truist, “Every midterm election year since 1946 has been followed by positive one-year stock returns. The biggest gain after a midterm election year was in 1954, at 34%. The average one-year gain has tallied 14.4%.”

Source: Truist

They went on to say, “Since 1950, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 6.6% during the fourth quarter of midterm-election years and advanced 84% of the time.”

I like hearing that!

Of course, that’s not the end of the story. Historically, stock market returns have also differed according to the make-up of Congress and which party may come out ahead.

U.S. Bank reports, “As of September 28, the House included 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies, while the Senate included 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats and two independents who caucus with Democrats.”

The following table of election outcomes vs. stock market returns reflects their findings.

White House + Congress ControlOutcomeAverage 3-Month S&P 500 Return During PeriodAverage 3-Month Return Relative to All Periods
D + DOne Party (D)2.20%-0.07%
D + RDivided3.85%1.57%
D + SplitDivided4.24%1.97%
R + DDivided1.19%-1.08%
R + ROne Party (R)2.89%0.62%
R + SplitDivided1.62%-0.66%
All One Party2.42%0.15%
Mixed Control2.17%-0.10%

Source: U.S. Bank

As you can see, for the most part, a divided Congress is better for investors. No one knows how this year’s elections will turn out, since the polls have proven seriously deficient in the past few elections. So, right now, it’s a guessing game.

Additional fun facts that sound positive for the markets, according to Fidelity:

Fourth-quarter rally: October and November average some of the strongest monthly returns of the four-year presidential cycle.
Congressional control scenarios: Gridlock (Split Congress) is often favored by markets as it reduces sweeping, disruptive policy changes.
Markets have responded more to changing levels of policy uncertainty rather than which party wins or loses.

But I can tell you that depending on which party wins the most seats, there is likely to be some governmental action that will affect the economy and the stock market.

U.S. Bank estimates that a Democratic House is the most likely outcome, which would make broad legislation harder to pass. Their next most likely scenario is Democratic control of the House and Senate, which could “block legislative priorities,” while Republicans maintaining full control of all three branches would give the White House “a clearer path for legislative priorities.”

Of course, there are a couple of other issues that the bank pointed out that may also affect the direction of both the economy and the markets.

Inflation and rate hikes. We’ve just seen our first rate hike by the Federal Reserve since July 2023. Inflation remains at a stubborn 3.4%, well above the Fed’s 2% target. Both of those factors weigh on economic strength, which eventually affects companies’ earnings. Right now, that has not been an issue, as FactSet reports that third-quarter earnings for the S&P 500 Index are expected to grow at a rate of 29.5%. But these are issues that need to be considered when reviewing your portfolio.

U.S. Bank also noted that there were numerous years where the economy overrode the impact of the election, specifically highlighting years that featured high inflation and rate hikes, with the 1990 results also affected by the Savings & Loan crisis and the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq.

1946 -10.9%
1966 -13.2%
1970 -14.4%
1990 -7.5%
2022 -14.6%
Returns cover the 12 months before each election.

War and policy shocks. Currently, we are afflicted by the Russia/Ukraine never-ending war (and don’t be surprised by additional repercussions as Russia continues a campaign of sneaking into other NATO countries), as well as the Iran War, which has sent fuel prices soaring in the U.S., significantly hurting consumer pocketbooks, and leaving less money for investment.

The Heritage Foundation noted this: “Sixth-year midterm elections tend to land a gut-punch on the party that has the White House. Presidents from Franklin Roosevelt (lost 72 seats) to Harry Truman (lost 28) and Dwight Eisenhower (lost 48) have suffered voter wrath in the sixth-year midterm elections.”

The one thing I know to be true is that markets don’t like uncertainty. Consequently, once the election is over, we’ll have a better understanding of which sectors and investment styles have the most potential.

In the meantime, here are a few portfolio tips to help you weather the next few weeks:

  • Reassess your near-, mid-, and long-term financial goals
  • Evaluate your risk tolerance
  • Consider rebalancing your portfolio to make sure it is adequately diversified
  • Emotions have no place in investing; it’s ok to love the company but not the stock!

3 ETFS for the Midterms

I don’t have a crystal ball to predict the election results, but here are three ETFs with Buy ratings that look attractive at this time:

State Street SPDR S&P Semiconductor ETF (XSD)
State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF (RLY)
State Street S&P 500 Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLE)

Happy investing, and don’t forget to VOTE!

data.title: The 20 Best-Performing Large-Cap Stocks of 2026
data.description:
The bull market has narrowed of late, with more than 70% of the S&P 500 now in correction territory (or worse). But despite that fact, the headline indexes are clearly reflecting an ongoing bull market, as the Nasdaq (up 17.9% so far this year) is hitting new all-time highs and the S&P 500 (up 13.2% YTD) is not far off its own.

At the same time, the Dow Jones Industrial Average, which my colleague Chris Preston has argued is more representative of the broader economy, has lagged (up only 5.8% in 2026). Add that all up, and we’re in an increasingly narrow bull market that is predominantly being driven by technology.

But for as much ink as has been spilled over the Magnificent 7 stocks over the last few years, the best-performing large-cap stocks have left all of them in the dust.

In fact, none of those seven stocks even made the following top 20 list, which sports a surprisingly high barrier to entry: Every single name on this list has doubled (or better) in 2026 alone.

[text_ad]

Here they are, in descending order of their year-to-date (YTD) returns.

The 20 Best-Performing Large-Cap Stocks by YTD Returns

1. Moderna (MRNA): 537%
2. Twist Bioscience (TWST): 524%
3. Sandisk (SNDK): 523%

As you can see, half of the top 10 (and four of the top five) companies on this list are biotech stocks (including the best-performing large-cap stock, Moderna), with most of the rest of the top 20 being made up of companies that are directly tied to the AI buildout in some form or another (including Bloom Energy, a fuel cell manufacturer that specializes in on-site power for data centers and the like).

The only exception is Marathon Petroleum (MPC), which is a petroleum refining and transportation company that’s directly benefiting from the disruption to the oil markets brought on by global conflict.

While you could frame this list as a tale of two bullish trends (AI and biotechnology), my personal opinion is that a large share of the outperformance by biotechs can be attributed to investors looking for down-the-food-chain beneficiaries of the growth of artificial intelligence.

The hyperscalers have had their time in the sun (and thus didn’t make this list), and the AI buildout is still minting winners (a handful of whom were in the top-20 list in 2025, including Sandisk, Lumentum, Bloom Energy and Micron). But investors are increasingly looking for the companies that will turn AI productivity gains (and new discoveries) into profits—and biotech stocks offer that potential (regardless of whether or not they end up realizing it further down the road).

So as 2026 enters the final stretch and you start looking ahead to 2027, keep your eyes peeled for companies that offer the same sort of potential.

data.title: Value Stocks Are Beating the Market—and Their Roster Is Growing
data.description:
Value stocks, as measured by the Vanguard Morningstar Value ETF (VTV), have quietly beaten the S&P 500 over the last year, rising 16.8% vs. gains of 15.4% for the large-cap index.

And that outperformance is even more pronounced when you compare VTV to the S&P 500 Equal-Weight Index (up 10.1% in the last 52 weeks), which normalizes the impact of the mega-cap tech stocks that have driven so much of the market’s return over the last three-plus years.

So while the headlines (and most portfolios) have been dominated by big tech and AI, tuning out that noise and focusing on undervalued stocks of solid companies would have netted you better returns.

The good news for investors is that the latest malaise in the market is actually making that even easier.

Under the surface, most of the stock market is currently in a correction. Per calculations from MarketWatch, 80% of the S&P 500 constituents are more than 10% below their 52-week highs, which is the threshold for “correction” territory.

And, as noted by Cabot Turnaround Letter Chief Analyst Clif Droke in a recent update to his subscribers, as of September 30, “more than 40% of S&P 500 stocks were at least 20% below their 52-week highs,” which pushes them past correction territory and firmly into a bear market.

[text_ad]

For most investors, a bear market in nearly half of large-cap stocks may seem like bad news, but for value-focused investors it just creates a larger roster of potentially undervalued stocks with room to outperform when the market rally resumes in earnest.

That’s not to say, of course, that every newly beaten-down stock is a market-beating opportunity. But that kind of broad weakness meaningfully increases the odds that appealing stocks are now trading at a discount.

And as a bit of context, it’s important to remember that the bull market is far from over – earnings growth is simply too strong for it to up and evaporate, even considering the myriad macro headwinds right now (namely sky-high bond yields, oil prices and mortgage rates). And I think another across-the-board rally is coming, whether it happens next week (the start of Q3 earnings season in October might be a good bet), or in November, after the midterms.

In the meantime, I will continue to look for stocks of companies that boast strong growth and offer disproportionate upside – my “growth at value prices” mantra.

In the last three months alone, and despite the recent sideways action in many stocks, three of our stocks have hit their upside price targets and been “retired” from the portfolio.

And just a few days ago, I added a new high-potential stock that’s fallen out of favor but boasts better than 60% upside from here.

Yes, the market has been frustrating, but soon the dam will break, the rally will resume and value stocks will do quite well, as they have for most of 2026.
